# The History of the Printing Press

*A research report based on English Wikipedia*

---

## 1. Introduction

The printing press is a device for applying pressure to an inked surface resting upon a print medium (typically paper or cloth), enabling the mass production of printed text. While the underlying concepts of printing originated in East Asia centuries earlier, the movable-type printing press developed by **Johannes Gutenberg** in Mainz, Germany (c. 1440–1450) is regarded as one of the most influential inventions in human history, triggering the "Printing Revolution" that reshaped European — and eventually global — society [1][2].

---

## 2. Before Gutenberg: East Asian Precedents

### 2.1 Woodblock Printing

Printing in East Asia predates Gutenberg's press by centuries:

- **China:** Woodblock printing developed during the Tang dynasty (7th century CE), initially used for textiles and later for text. The **Diamond Sutra (868 CE)**, discovered at Dunhuang, is the world's oldest surviving dated printed book [1][3].
- **Japan:** The *Hyakumantō Darani* (c. 764–770) was among the earliest mass-printed texts [3].
- **Korea:** The **Tripitaka Koreana** (1236–1251) comprises over 81,000 woodblocks at Haeinsa Temple — one of the most complete Buddhist canons ever produced [4].

### 2.2 Movable Type in China

The world's **first movable type system** was invented by **Bi Sheng** (c. 970–1051), a commoner artisan of the Northern Song dynasty, around **1041–1048 CE**. He used individual characters carved from baked clay/porcelain, set into an iron frame and secured with pine resin and wax. His method is documented in Shen Kuo's *Dream Pool Essays* (1088). Later Chinese refinements included **Wang Zhen's** wooden movable type and rotating typecase (c. 1297) and **Hua Sui's** bronze type (c. 1490) [3][5].

### 2.3 Metal Movable Type in Korea

Korea developed the most sustained pre-Gutenberg metal-type program:

- The *Goryeosa* records the casting of bronze type in **1234** to print the *Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun*, though no copies survive [6].
- The ***Jikji*** (1377), printed with movable metal type at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju, is the **oldest extant book printed with metal movable type** — predating the Gutenberg Bible by 78 years. It is held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France and was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2001 [7].
- In 1403, King Taejong of Joseon established a national foundry (Jujaso) for government type casting, and under **King Sejong the Great**, refined typefaces were cast and **Hangul** (1443) — an alphabet exceptionally suited to movable type — was created [6].

Whether Gutenberg's invention was influenced by East Asian printing via the Silk Road or was wholly independent remains debated by scholars [3][8]. Notably, these East Asian systems did not achieve mass production, partly because Chinese writing's thousands of logographic characters made type-based printing less economical than alphabetic scripts [3].

---

## 3. Gutenberg's Invention (c. 1440–1455)

### 3.1 The Inventor

**Johannes Gutenberg** (c. 1400–1468), a goldsmith from Mainz, began experiments in **Strasbourg around 1440** and perfected his system in Mainz by about 1450 [2][9]. His genius lay not in inventing printing itself, but in **combining existing technologies into a complete, practical, scalable printing system** [2][8].

### 3.2 Key Innovations

1. **Metal movable type and the hand mould** — An adjustable mould enabled rapid, identical casting of individual type pieces in a durable **lead–tin–antimony alloy** (chosen for its low melting point, clean mold-filling, and durability). The punch–matrix–casting workflow remained standard for roughly 500 years [2][8].
2. **Oil-based ink** — Water-based inks used for woodblocks did not adhere to metal, so Gutenberg formulated a sticky ink of boiled **linseed oil** mixed with soot/lampblack that bonded to metal type and transferred cleanly to paper or vellum [2][10].
3. **Adaptation of the screw press** — He adapted the screw press used for wine, olives, and papermaking to apply firm, **even pressure across the whole page**, superior to the rubbing methods of woodblock printing. A movable bed/carriage allowed quick page changes and high throughput [2][8].

### 3.3 The Gutenberg Bible

Financed by loans from **Johann Fust** (800 guilders, later 1,600 more), Gutenberg produced the **42-line Gutenberg Bible (c. 1454–1455)** — the first major book printed with movable metal type in Europe [2][9][11]:

- Latin Vulgate text, 42 lines per page in two columns, two volumes totaling ~1,286 pages
- Edition of roughly **180 copies** (~135–150 on paper, 30–45 on vellum)
- **Textura (blackletter)** typeface with ~290 distinct sorts, designed to mimic hand-copied manuscripts
- Rubrication and decorated initials added by hand; paper imported from Italian mills
- Copies sold for **30 florins** — about three years' wages for a clerk
- **~49 copies survive today** (about 21 complete); notable copies are held by the Library of Congress, the British Library, and the Morgan Library & Museum [11]

In a **1455 lawsuit**, Fust won control of most of Gutenberg's equipment and continued printing with **Peter Schöffer** [2][9].

### 3.4 Productivity Leap

A single Gutenberg-style press could produce roughly **3,600 pages per workday**, compared with only a few pages by a hand copyist — a productivity gain of several orders of magnitude that made mass production of text feasible for the first time [1][12].

---

## 4. Spread Across Europe (1450–1600)

### 4.1 Diffusion

The **1462 Sack of Mainz** dispersed German printers, accelerating the technology's spread [1]. Carried largely by German craftsmen, printing reached [1][13]:

| Region | First Press |
|---|---|
| Italy | Subiaco, 1465; Venice, 1469 |
| France | Paris, 1470 |
| Spain | c. 1472–74 |
| England | Westminster (William Caxton), 1476 |

By **1500**, presses operated in **more than 250 European towns and cities**, producing an estimated **20 million volumes**. Books printed before 1501 are called **incunabula** — roughly 27,000–30,000 known distinct editions [1][14]. The 16th century saw an estimated **150–200 million copies** printed, with presses in nearly every major European city by 1600 [1][12].

**Venice** became Europe's leading printing center. **Aldus Manutius** (Aldine Press, founded c. 1494) pioneered **italic type** (1501) and pocket-sized, affordable editions of the classics [1][12].

### 4.2 The Printing Revolution and Its Cultural Impact

Historians — most influentially **Elizabeth Eisenstein** — frame print as the engine of transformations across early modern Europe [1][12]:

- **The Reformation:** Luther's **95 Theses (1517)** spread throughout Germany within about two weeks and across Europe within two months. Luther was the era's most published author — roughly **one-fifth to one-third of all German books printed between 1518 and 1525** were his. Cheap pamphlets (*Flugschriften*) carried Reformation arguments to mass audiences, and Luther's **German Bible** (New Testament 1522; complete 1534) democratized access to scripture. Historians such as Andrew Pettegree argue the Reformation was the first mass-media movement, unlikely to have succeeded without print [15].
- **The Renaissance:** Print accelerated the dissemination of recovered classical texts, enabled textual criticism and philology (e.g., Erasmus's 1516 Greek New Testament), and created a trans-European "republic of letters" [12][16].
- **The Scientific Revolution:** Exact reproduction of diagrams, maps, tables, and data underpinned the work of Copernicus, Vesalius, and others [12].
- **Language and literacy:** Printing standardized vernacular languages, strengthened them alongside Latin, and expanded literacy and the professions of authorship and publishing [12].

### 4.3 Censorship and Early News

Authorities responded to print's power with censorship — most notably the Catholic Church's **Index Librorum Prohibitorum (1559)** and England's Licensing Acts [1][15]. The first printed **weekly newspaper** appeared in Strasbourg in **1605** — Johann Carolus's *Relation* [1].

---

## 5. Industrial-Era and Modern Advances

Gutenberg's wooden screw press remained essentially unchanged for **~350 years** before mechanization transformed printing [1]:

| Year | Innovation | Inventor | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1800 | All-iron hand press | Lord Stanhope | Larger platen, less effort required [1] |
| 1814 | **Steam-powered cylinder press** | Friedrich Koenig (with Andreas Bauer) | *The Times* of London printed by steam on 29 November 1814 — ~1,100 sheets/hour vs. ~250 by hand; Koenig & Bauer (founded 1817) remains the world's oldest operating press manufacturer [17] |
| 1843–47 | **Rotary press** | Richard March Hoe | Type curved on a rotating cylinder; ~8,000–10,000 impressions/hour ("Hoe Lightning" presses) [18] |
| 1863–65 | **Web-fed rotary press** | William Bullock | Continuous paper rolls, automatic feeding, printing both sides simultaneously — backbone of mass-circulation newspapers [18] |
| 1884–86 | **Linotype** | Ottmar Mergenthaler | Keyboard-operated machine casting entire lines of type as single metal slugs; first installed at the *New York Tribune* (1886); Thomas Edison reportedly called it "the eighth wonder of the world" [19] |
| 1796–98 | **Lithography** | Alois Senefelder | Chemical printing foundation for later offset methods [20] |
| 1904 | **Offset lithography** | Ira Washington Rubel | Rubber-blanket transfer produced sharper impressions; became the **dominant commercial printing method of the 20th century** [20] |

The 20th century brought phototypesetting, **laser printing** (Xerox, 1970s), and **desktop publishing** (1980s) — culminating in what has been called the "digital printing revolution" [1][18].

---

## 6. Conclusion

The history of the printing press spans nearly two millennia, from Chinese woodblocks and Bi Sheng's ceramic movable type (c. 1040) to Korea's metal-type *Jikji* (1377), through Gutenberg's integrated system (c. 1450), and onward through steam, rotary, Linotype, and offset technologies to today's digital publishing. Gutenberg's decisive contribution was synthesizing movable metal type, the hand mould, oil-based ink, and the screw press into a scalable system that collapsed the cost of reproducing text. In doing so, it enabled the Reformation, accelerated the Renaissance and Scientific Revolution, standardized vernacular languages, and laid the foundation for modern mass communication and universal literacy [1][2][12].

---

## Movable type printing in East Asia: Bi Sheng, woodblock printing, Jikji, Korean metal type - Wikipedia
# Movable Type Printing in East Asia — Summary

## Woodblock Printing (the precursor)

Woodblock printing (xylography) developed in Tang-dynasty China by the 7th century CE and spread to Korea and Japan [1]. Key milestones include:

- **Diamond Sutra (868 CE)** — the world's oldest surviving dated printed book, woodblock-printed and found at Dunhuang [1].
- **Hyakumantō Darani (Japan, c. 764–770)** — among the earliest mass-printed texts [1].
- **Tripitaka Koreana (Korea, 1236–1251)** — over 81,000 woodblocks at Haeinsa Temple, one of the most complete Buddhist canons [2].

Woodblock printing remained dominant in East Asia partly because Chinese writing uses thousands of unique logographic characters, making type-based printing less economical than in alphabetic scripts [1][3].

## Bi Sheng and Ceramic Movable Type (China, c. 1040s)

Bi Sheng (毕昇, c. 970–1051), a commoner artisan of the Northern Song dynasty, invented the **world's first movable type printing system around 1041–1048**, using individual characters carved from baked clay/porcelain [3][4]. His method is documented in Shen Kuo's *Dream Pool Essays* (Mengxi Bitan, 1088): type pieces were set into an iron frame, secured with pine resin and wax, heated to fix them for printing, then reheated to remove and reuse the type [4]. Later Chinese refinements included **Wang Zhen's wooden movable type and rotating typecase (c. 1297–1298)**, described in his treatise appended to the *Nong Shu*, and **Hua Sui's bronze type (c. 1490)** during the Ming dynasty [3][5].

## Jikji — Oldest Extant Metal-Type-Printed Book (Korea, 1377)

***Jikji Simche Yojeol*** ("Anthology of Great Buddhist Priests' Zen Teachings") was printed with **movable metal type at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju, Goryeo-dynasty Korea, in July 1377** — making it the oldest extant book printed with metal movable type, predating Gutenberg's Bible (c. 1455) by 78 years [6]. Its colophon explicitly records the metal-type printing. The surviving second volume is held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, and the book was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2001 [6][7].

## Korean Metal Type Tradition

Korea (Goryeo and Joseon dynasties) developed the most sustained pre-Gutenberg metal-type program:

- The *Goryeosa* records the casting of bronze type in **1234** to print the *Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun* (Prescribed Ritual Texts), though no copies survive [2][7].
- In **1403**, King Taejong of Joseon established a national foundry (Jujaso) for government type casting [7].
- Under **King Sejong the Great**, successive refined typefaces were cast (e.g., Gyemi type, 1434), and the creation of **Hangul (1443)** — an alphabet of ~24 letters — was exceptionally well suited to movable-type printing [7][8].
- Metal type was favored in Korea partly due to scarcity of suitable wood and strong royal patronage [7].

## Historical Significance

Gutenberg's mid-15th-century press (c. 1440s–1455) introduced movable type to Europe; whether it was influenced by East Asian printing via the Silk Road or was an independent invention remains debated by scholars [3][9].

## Gutenberg Bible and Gutenberg's innovations (screw press, oil-based ink, metal movable type) - Wikipedia
# Gutenberg Bible and Gutenberg's Innovations — Research Summary

## The Gutenberg Bible (42-line Bible, "B42")

- Printed in **Mainz, Germany, c. 1454–1455**; widely regarded as the **first major book produced with movable metal type in Europe** and the beginning of the age of printed books [1][2].
- Text: the **Latin Vulgate**; each page contains **42 lines** set in **two columns** (hence "42-line Bible") [1].
- Physical format: **two volumes, ~1,286 pages**; approximately **180 copies** were printed — roughly **135–150 on paper and 30–45 on vellum** [1].
- Typeface: **Textura (blackletter)**, with roughly **290 distinct sorts** (including ligatures and abbreviations) designed to mimic the appearance of a hand-copied manuscript [1][2].
- **Rubrication** (red headings) and decorated initials were added by hand after printing; paper was imported from Italian mills [1].
- Copies reportedly sold for **30 florins** — about three years' wages for a clerk [1].
- **~49 copies survive today**, of which about **21 are complete**; notable copies are held by the Library of Congress (a complete vellum copy), the British Library, and the Morgan Library & Museum (three copies) [1].

## Gutenberg's Key Innovations (c. 1440–1455)

Johannes Gutenberg (c. 1400–1468), a goldsmith from Mainz, did not invent printing itself — woodblock printing and movable type existed earlier in East Asia (e.g., Bi Sheng's ceramic type in 11th-century China; Korea's Jikji, printed with metal type in 1377). His achievement was combining and perfecting technologies into a **practical, scalable printing system** [2][3][4].

1. **Metal movable type and the hand mould**
   - Developed an **adjustable hand mould** enabling rapid, standardized casting of individual type pieces — the punch–matrix–casting workflow remained standard for ~500 years [2][3].
   - Type was cast in a **lead–tin–antimony alloy**, chosen for its low melting point, ability to fill a mold cleanly, and durability under repeated pressing [2][3].

2. **Adaptation of the screw press**
   - Adapted the **screw press used for wine, olives, and paper** to printing, applying firm, **even pressure across the whole page** — superior to the rubbing methods used with woodblocks and East Asian printing [2][4].
   - A movable bed/carriage allowed quick insertion and removal of pages, enabling high throughput [2][4].

3. **Oil-based ink**
   - Water-based inks used for woodblocks did not adhere to metal type, so Gutenberg formulated a **sticky, oil-based ink** (likely boiled **linseed oil** mixed with soot/lampblack and other additives) that bonded to metal and transferred cleanly to paper or vellum [2][5].

## Historical Context and Impact

- Gutenberg financed the project partly through loans from **Johann Fust** (800 guilders, later 1,600 more). In a **1455 lawsuit**, Fust won control of the equipment and partnered with **Peter Schöffer**; some scholars debate Gutenberg's exact role in completing the 42-line Bible, though it is traditionally attributed to him [1][2].
- The printing system spread rapidly: by 1500, presses operated in **over 250 European cities**, producing an estimated **20 million volumes** (the "incunabula" period) [4][6].
- Cheap, uniform printed books enabled the **Printing Revolution**, accelerating the Renaissance, the Reformation (e.g., rapid dissemination of Luther's writings), and the scientific revolution [2][4].

## Spread of printing press across Europe 15th-16th centuries, printing revolution, impact on Reformation and Renaissance - Wikipedia
# The Printing Press in Europe: Spread, Revolution, and Cultural Impact

## Origins

- Johannes Gutenberg developed the movable-type printing press in Mainz, Germany, around **1440–1450**, combining metal movable type, a hand mould for casting type, oil-based ink, and an adapted screw press [1].
- The **Gutenberg Bible** (42-line Bible) was completed around **1455** in an edition of roughly 180 copies, marking the start of the printed book era in Europe [1][2].

## Spread Across Europe (1450–1500)

- The technology spread rapidly from Mainz, carried largely by German printers: **Italy** (Subiaco 1465, Venice 1469), **Paris** (1470), **Spain**, the **Low Countries**, **England** (William Caxton at Westminster, 1476), and **Central and Northern Europe** [3].
- By **1500**, presses were operating in more than **250–270 European towns and cities** [3][4].
- **Venice** became Europe's leading printing center; Aldus Manutius's Aldine Press (founded c. 1494) pioneered italic type and portable, affordable editions of the classics [5].
- Books printed before 1501 are called **incunabula** — roughly 27,000–30,000 distinct editions, totaling an estimated **8–20 million copies** [4].

## The Printing Revolution

- A single print shop could produce around **3,600 pages per day**, versus only a few pages by a hand copyist — a productivity leap of several orders of magnitude [1][6].
- Book prices fell dramatically (estimates of ~80% or more), making books accessible far beyond clergy and wealthy elites [6].
- The 16th century saw an estimated **150–200 million books printed** (Febvre & Martin's classic estimate), with presses in nearly every major European city by 1600 [6].
- Consequences included standardized texts, growth of book fairs (notably Frankfurt), the rise of authorship and publishing as professions, expanding literacy, and the strengthening of **vernacular languages** alongside Latin [6].

## Impact on the Reformation

- The press is widely regarded as a decisive enabler of the Reformation. Luther's **95 Theses (1517)** were printed and spread throughout Germany within about two weeks and across Europe within two months [7].
- Luther was the era's most published author: roughly **one-fifth to one-third of all books printed in Germany between 1518 and 1525** were by him [7].
- Cheap pamphlets (**Flugschriften**) — numbering in the thousands of editions — carried Reformation arguments to a mass audience; Luther's **German Bible** (New Testament 1522; complete Bible 1534) democratized scripture access [7][8].
- The Catholic Church responded with censorship mechanisms, notably the **Index Librorum Prohibitorum** (1559) [8].
- Historians (e.g., Andrew Pettegree) argue the Reformation was the first mass media movement — without print, it likely could not have succeeded [7].

## Impact on the Renaissance

- Printing accelerated the dissemination of **recovered classical texts** and humanist scholarship from Italy northward, standardizing editions of authors such as Cicero, Virgil, and the Greek classics (championed by Aldus Manutius) [5][9].
- It enabled **textual criticism and philology** — scholars could compare editions, producing more accurate texts (e.g., Erasmus's 1516 Greek New Testament) [9].
- Print created a trans-European **republic of letters**, allowing humanists to correspond, publish, and build on each other's work far faster than manuscript culture allowed [9].

## Broader Legacy

- The press underpinned the **Scientific Revolution** by enabling exact reproduction of diagrams, maps, tables, and data (Copernicus, Vesalius) [6].
- Elizabeth Eisenstein's influential thesis frames print as the engine of the "printing revolution" that made the Renaissance, Reformation, and Scientific Revolution possible at scale [6].

## Industrial-era printing advances: steam-powered press, rotary press, linotype, offset printing - Wikipedia
# Industrial-Era Printing Advances — Summary

## 1. Steam-Powered Press [1]
- **Inventor:** Friedrich Koenig, a German printer, built the first steam-powered printing press in London, patented in 1810, with mechanical partner Andreas Bauer.
- **Milestone:** On **29 November 1814**, *The Times* of London was printed entirely by steam power — the first newspaper printed this way. Output reached roughly **1,100 sheets per hour** vs. ~250 on a hand press.
- **Design:** Used a reciprocating flat bed with an impression cylinder, driven by steam rather than hand leverage.
- **Legacy:** Koenig and Bauer founded the firm **Koenig & Bauer in 1817**, still the world's oldest operating printing-press manufacturer.

## 2. Rotary Press [2]
- **Inventor:** American **Richard March Hoe** patented the rotary press in **1843**; it entered commercial use in **1847** (first used by the *Philadelphia Public Ledger*). Type was curved on a rotating cylinder, eliminating the slow flat bed — press speeds jumped to **~8,000–10,000 impressions/hour** ("Hoe Lightning" presses).
- **Key refinement:** **William Bullock** (c. 1863–1865) created a **web-fed rotary press** using a continuous paper roll, with automatic feeding and printing on both sides simultaneously. Bullock died in 1867 from an injury caused by his own press.
- **Impact:** Web-fed rotary presses became the backbone of mass-circulation newspapers; later models printed, cut, and folded in one pass.

## 3. Linotype [3]
- **Inventor:** German-American **Ottmar Mergenthaler**, patented **1884**; first commercial installation at the *New York Tribune* in **1886**.
- **Function:** A keyboard-operated machine that assembles brass matrices and casts an **entire line of type as a single metal slug** ("line-o'-type") from a hot lead alloy, then automatically redistributes the matrices.
- **Impact:** One operator could set type several times faster than hand compositors, transforming newspaper and book production. Thomas Edison reportedly called it "the eighth wonder of the world." (Its competitor, the Monotype, cast individual characters.)

## 4. Offset Printing [4]
- **Roots:** Built on lithography, invented by **Alois Senefelder (1796–98)**.
- **First offset press:** **Robert Barclay (1875, England)**, printing on metal (tin) via a rubber-covered impression cylinder.
- **Paper offset:** **Ira Washington Rubel (1903–04)** accidentally discovered that a rubber blanket produced a sharper second impression and built the first paper-fed offset press in **1904**; Caspar Hermann developed similar rotary-offset designs concurrently.
- **Advantages:** The soft rubber blanket conforms to rough surfaces, extends plate life, and yields consistent high-quality images at high speed — making **offset lithography the dominant commercial printing method of the 20th century**.

### Overall arc
Steam power mechanized printing (1814) → rotary cylinders multiplied speed (1847) → the Linotype automated typesetting (1886) → offset lithography enabled cheap, high-quality mass reproduction (1904 onward), together driving the era of mass-circulation newspapers and books.
